title: A handful of sand
hookLine: a commentary story: each morning Rahula took up a handful of sand and wished for as much advice as there were grains in his hand

cards: There's a sentence that can make a stomach drop: can I give you some feedback? Rahula, the commentaries say, went looking for it.
Every morning, the story goes, he stepped out of his dwelling, bent down, and scooped up a handful of sand.
Then he made a wish over it: may I receive today, from the Blessed One and from my teachers, as much advice as there are grains of sand in my hand. Not as much praise. Not as much comfort.
As much advice. A boy who asks to be corrected, every day, by the handful.

teach.b: First, the list he's on. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha names disciples who stand out, each for one quality, and Rahula is foremost among those who love the training.

Not the wisest, not the strongest: the one who most wants to learn. The handful of sand is the commentary's way of showing what that looks like on an ordinary morning. Second, why it's harder than it sounds.
Advice means someone has noticed what you're doing wrong. It's easy to want the teaching and skip the correction.
Rahula treats correction as something to be gathered, like alms, like water.

teach.h: DON'T LET CLOSENESS DULL THE TEACHER.
teach.b: Third, living close to a teacher. In a short discourse in the Sutta Nipata, the Buddha asks Rahula: does living with a wise man all the time make you look down on him?

It's a real danger; familiarity can make a teacher ordinary, and their advice easy to wave away. Rahula says no, he honors the one who holds up the torch for people. The sand is that answer, lived out every morning.
Fourth, what it asks of an ordinary day. Nobody could actually receive that much advice in a day, and the story knows it. The point isn't the number.
It's the open hand. Last year we heard how his learning ended, with full awakening.
The commentaries say this is how it went, day by day: with sand.

how: Rahula is remembered in Theravada teaching as the model of a student eager to train, and the handful-of-sand story is told to novices and lay students as a picture of welcoming correction.

o: one who has finished the training

s: Rahula wished for as much praise as there were grains of sand
the story says advice: as much instruction from his teachers as the grains in his hand.
the Anguttara names Rahula foremost among those who love the training
each great disciple is named for one quality; his is eagerness to train.
the handful of sand comes from the suttas themselves
it's a commentary story; the suttas give the title it illustrates.

games.q: you're Rahula. it's morning, and you've scooped up a handful of sand. what do you wish for?
o: as many years of life as these grains.
as much advice as these grains.
as many students as these grains.
games.why: the commentaries say he wished to receive, that day, as much advice from the Buddha and his teachers as there were grains in his hand.

practice: Open one hand on your knee, palm up, as if it held sand, and bring to mind someone whose view you trust and who sees you clearly. Imagine asking them: what's one thing I could do better?
Notice what the body does as you picture their answer, and let the hand stay open anyway.

wordCard.voice: Sikkhakama, one who loves the training. The quality the Buddha named Rahula foremost in, pictured by his daily handful of sand. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sikkhakama: one who loves the training. Rahula is named foremost in it.

carryVoice: Your line: as much as sand. The open hand matters more than the number. Day seven hundred fifty-one, done.
